item.title: Where the Smokies Turn to Ice
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Each January, Haywood County, North Carolina, turns its abundance of mountain water into an unexpected winter spectacle during Visit Haywood Ice Fest Weekend. Set amid the Great Smoky Mountains, the county is one of the nation’s few headwater counties, and the annual celebration transforms that connection to water into art, with professional ice carvers shaping massive blocks of ice during live demonstrations. After dark, illuminated sculptures add another dimension to the festival, while Canton’s seasonal ice rink brings skating, ice hockey and slides into the mix.

The celebration extends beyond the carving demonstrations. In downtown Waynesville, the Ice Block Party brings Main Street to life with ice sculptures, late-opening local businesses and seasonal food specials. At Lake Junaluska, the Ice Garden offers a quieter experience, with glowing snowflakes, icicles and ice lanterns creating an atmospheric evening landscape. Winter also provides a different perspective on the surrounding mountains, from birding walks and waterfall hikes to frozen cascades and mountain views. For more active pursuits, Cataloochee Ski Area offers skiing and snowboarding, while nearby Tube World adds snow tubing to the itinerary.

The Curated Take: Haywood County’s winter appeal is less about simply finding snow and more about seeing the landscape transformed by the season. The Ice Fest gives visitors a reason to engage with the destination through art, local businesses and the natural character of the Smokies, while the surrounding experiences make it possible to build a winter escape that moves between lively mountain towns and quieter landscapes.

item.title: A Yacht-Sized Way to See the Caribbean This Winter
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For travelers looking beyond the traditional Caribbean cruise this winter, SeaDream Yacht Club is offering a more intimate way to move through the region. Its 2026–27 season runs from late November through April 2027, with 112-guest SeaDream I and SeaDream II sailing from gateways including Palm Beach, San Juan and St. Thomas. Rather than concentrating on the Caribbean’s largest ports, itineraries weave through destinations including St. Barths, Jost van Dyke, Virgin Gorda, Bequia, St. Lucia and Îles des Saintes, along with smaller harbors and less-visited islands.

The yacht experience is designed to extend beyond the ship itself. Depending on the sailing, guests can snorkel and sail through the British Virgin Islands, explore Virgin Gorda’s Baths, hike in St. Lucia or spend a day discovering the beaches and villages of Îles des Saintes. Back onboard, SeaDream can lower its watersports Marina directly into the Caribbean for swimming, kayaking and paddleboarding, while select sailings feature the signature Champagne & Caviar Splash, an indulgent beachside experience. The appeal is less about seeing the Caribbean from a large ship and more about moving through it with the scale and flexibility of a private yacht: unpack once, wake somewhere new and spend the day exploring at a more intimate pace.

The Curated Take: The Caribbean is hardly short on cruise options, but SeaDream’s small-ship approach speaks to travelers who want the convenience of cruising without sacrificing a sense of place. With smaller harbors, yacht-level access to the water and time ashore across a mix of familiar and less-obvious islands, the experience offers a different lens on a region many travelers think they already know.

item.title: A Winter Lodge Lands in the Heart of Manhattan
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Winter in New York City gets a cozy, theatrical makeover at Kimpton Hotel Eventi, where the Winter Lodge Suite transforms a Manhattan stay into an immersive seasonal escape. Set at the crossroads of NoMad and Chelsea, the one- and two-bedroom suites are dressed in flocked décor, faux eucalyptus and fir garlands, silver accents and other winter-inspired details, creating the feel of a private alpine retreat without leaving the city.

The experience extends beyond the suite with coordinated winter pajamas for guests and furry companions, ice skating tickets and rentals, an après-skate amenity and a complimentary round of winter drinks at Eventi’s Back Bar. Accommodating groups of up to six or eight depending on the suite, the concept offers a particularly playful way to experience New York during the colder months, pairing the energy of Manhattan with the comforts and rituals of a winter lodge.

The Curated Take: There is something appealing about treating winter in New York as a destination experience rather than something to escape. The Winter Lodge Suite leans fully into the season, creating an intimate, nostalgic counterpoint to the city outside and making the hotel itself part of the winter itinerary.

item.title: The Mekong as the Road Through Laos
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
A new journey through Laos is making the Mekong itself part of the itinerary. The Bohème Journey, from Avani Hotels & Resorts, links the newly opened Avani+ Lanexang Vientiane Hotel with five nights aboard the luxury cruiser Bohème by Mekong Kingdoms before concluding at Avani+ Luang Prabang. The six-day passage connects the contemporary Lao capital with riverside communities, traditional crafts and the UNESCO-listed former royal capital of Luang Prabang.

The journey begins in Vientiane, where the 197-room Avani+ Lanexang overlooks the Mekong and Chao Anouvong Park. Its location provides an easy introduction to the capital’s temples, markets, museums and riverside life, including landmarks such as Patuxai, Pha That Luang and Wat Sisaket. From there, guests travel to Pak Lay to board Bohème and begin the upstream journey toward northern Laos. The 164-foot cruiser accommodates no more than 26 guests across 13 cabins, with Lao textiles and polished woodwork shaping its interiors. Days combine shore excursions with time on the river, including visits to villages known for Saa paper-making, weaving and pottery, passage through the Xayaboury Dam locks, an ethical wildlife experience at Elephant Sanctuary Laos and a visit to the turquoise pools of Kuang Si Waterfalls. On board, guests can take part in Lao cooking and cocktail workshops, enjoy meals and sunset cocktails, or simply watch the landscape change from the sun deck.

The journey concludes in Luang Prabang, where Avani+ Luang Prabang occupies a heritage-inspired building opposite the Night Market. The 53-room property puts travelers within walking distance of the Royal Palace, Mount Phousi, Wat Xieng Thong and the morning market, while experiences such as the town’s daily almsgiving tradition offer another connection to local culture. With arrival through Vientiane and departure from Luang Prabang, the itinerary also allows travelers to experience two very different sides of Laos without retracing their route.

The Curated Take: The most compelling element here is the decision to make the Mekong the journey rather than simply something to see along the way. Moving at river pace creates a natural progression from city to village to heritage town, while the combination of craft, food, wildlife and local encounters gives travelers a fuller understanding of Laos. It is a particularly appealing approach for travelers who want luxury to facilitate deeper access to a destination rather than separate them from it.

item.title: Winter by Rail and Light in Virginia’s Richmond Region
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Winter takes on a particularly festive character in Virginia’s Richmond Region, where illuminated gardens, historic railroad tracks and a brand-new seasonal attraction offer different ways to experience the area during the holidays. From Richmond’s urban energy to the small-town charm of Ashland, the region combines traditional Christmas atmosphere with experiences that feel distinctly local.

At Lewis Ginter Botanical Garden, the annual Dominion Energy GardenFest of Lights transforms the grounds into a walk-through display illuminated by more than a million lights. The experience combines large-scale light installations with botanical displays and seasonal activities, turning the garden into an evening destination that draws visitors from beyond the Richmond area.

In Ashland, known as “The Center of the Universe,” the holiday season unfolds along an active railroad corridor. Light Up the Tracks creates a mile-long display of lights along the historic rail line, while visitors can shop and dine downtown and watch trains pass directly through the center of town. The combination of a working railway, small-town streets and holiday lights gives the experience a sense of place that goes beyond a conventional Christmas display.

New for 2026, WINTERWORLD brings a more contemporary winter experience to Richmond’s CarMax Park. The seasonal attraction will feature outdoor ice skating, a Ferris wheel, festive food and beverages, a holiday village, immersive lighting installations and one of Richmond’s tallest Christmas trees, transforming the entertainment venue into a destination of its own for the winter season.

The Curated Take: The Richmond Region’s winter appeal comes from the variety of ways it interprets the season. GardenFest offers an immersive evening surrounded by nature, Ashland turns an active railroad into the backdrop for a small-town Christmas, and WINTERWORLD introduces a new urban-scale celebration. Together, they make the region interesting for travelers who want holiday traditions, but also want those traditions to feel connected to the character of the place they are visiting.

item.title: Inside Niseko’s New Generation of Luxury Chalets
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Niseko has become one of Asia’s most coveted ski destinations, pairing legendary Hokkaido powder with Japanese hospitality, cuisine and culture. As the destination has matured, so has its luxury accommodation scene, with private chalets offering the space and seclusion of a mountain residence alongside the kind of personalized service more commonly associated with a five-star hotel. The Luxe Nomad, Asia-Pacific’s largest luxury vacation rental management company, manages several of Niseko’s most exclusive residences.

Tsubasa Chalet at Hanaridge puts groups of up to 12 within minutes of Hanazono Resort, with five bedrooms, uninterrupted views of Mount Yotei and a private indoor-outdoor natural onsen. The residence also features a gym, chef’s kitchen, butler service and two chauffeured vehicles, creating a highly serviced retreat for larger families or groups. The chalet was named Japan’s Best Ski Chalet at the World Ski Awards.

Corniche Hirafu takes a more contemporary approach in the heart of Hirafu, positioned along the area’s coveted Millionaires’ Row just moments from the gondola. The four-bedroom residence combines 19-foot ceilings and panoramic mountain views with a private natural onsen, sauna, cold plunge and rooftop sky terraces. A dedicated ski room and butler service add another layer of convenience for guests who want to move easily between the mountain and their private retreat.

Meigetsu Aki Niseko, which debuted in 2025, offers another take on contemporary chalet living in Upper Hirafu, close to the ski lifts. Designed with families and groups in mind, the four-bedroom residence includes a private sauna and cold plunge, rooftop terrace, chef’s kitchen, wine cooler, elevator and garage. Butler service and two chauffeured vehicles further distinguish the property, while its modern design creates a comfortable base for exploring Niseko in winter.

The Curated Take: What distinguishes Niseko’s luxury chalet scene is the way it combines the privacy of a private residence with a level of service that removes much of the logistics from an international ski holiday. Private onsens and wellness spaces bring a distinctly Japanese dimension to the experience, while butlers and chauffeured transportation allow guests to focus on the mountain rather than the practicalities surrounding it. Together, these residences reflect a destination that has evolved from a powder-skiing discovery into a sophisticated luxury escape in its own right.

item.title: Rails into the Wild
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Two thousand wild beluga whales whistle through the icy thaws of Hudson Bay, while polar bears roam the vast, wind-scoured permafrost of the Canadian subarctic. Thousands of miles away, ancient glaciers cling to sheer granite peaks, carving vertical gorges through the silent high passes of the Swiss Alps. These are places defined by their untamed scale—landscapes so uncompromising that vast stretches remain entirely untouched by roads or highways.

To enter these worlds on human terms, steel tracks are carved directly into the elements. They snake across frozen permafrost, cling to rock-hewn cliffs, scale 196 stone bridges, and plunge through 55 mountain tunnels. Along these iron lines, the train glides—a quiet, panoramic sanctuary cutting through terrain where civilization falls away. Choosing the rails turns transit into a front-row seat to the planet’s most dramatic environmental shifts.

To the Edge of the Tundra: The VIA Rail Hudson Bay Line

Churchill, Manitoba sits on the edge of the subarctic wilderness, completely severed from Canada’s highway system. The two-day VIA Rail line from Winnipeg is the only overland way in, cutting a thousand miles through shifting biomes. Outside your window, flat golden prairies melt into dense spruce boreal forest, which gradually thins into the raw, open tundra.

Step off the platform into Churchill, and the wild meets you instantly. In high summer (July and August), migrating belugas fill the Churchill River estuary, allowing you to paddle alongside them in kayaks. By autumn (October and November), the tundra freezes and wild polar bears gather along the coast waiting for Hudson Bay to lock into ice. Deep winter (February and March) brings crisp nights beneath the auroral oval, where green ribbons of northern lights dance overhead while you warm up at the timber-framed Lazy Bear Lodge. Before setting out from Winnipeg, anchor your departure at the historic Fort Garry Hotel for a quiet nod to classic railway luxury.

High-Altitude Iron: Graubünden’s Alpine Tracks

In eastern Switzerland, the narrow-gauge tracks of the Glacier Express and Bernina Express hang suspended over sheer chasms, threading through the high passes of Graubünden. Known as the “slowest express train in the world,” the Glacier Express forces you to surrender your watch, taking eight unhurried hours between Zermatt and St. Moritz as towering gorges, icy waterfalls, and timbered alpine hamlets slide past.

Its sibling, the Bernina Express, climbs past the blue ice of eternal glaciers at Ospizio Bernina before dropping precipitously into palm-fringed Italian valleys. Boarding between December and March wraps you in a warm glass observatory while snowstorms blanket the peaks, while alpine summer transforms the line into a gateway for high-altitude wilderness hikes. Base yourself at Badrutt’s Palace or the Kulm Hotel in St. Moritz to watch the morning mist clear over the lake before stepping directly onto the train platform and gliding straight into the mountain wild.

item.title: The Geography of Stillness: 4 Escapes Where Landscape Is the Ritual
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Modern wellness has a habit of boxing itself in. We retreat into windowless treatment rooms, cocooned in synthetic white linens, listening to recorded rainfall while a diffuser attempts to replicate a forest we chose to leave behind. It is a sterile approach to restoration—one that treats the body as a machine to be serviced rather than an organism built to resonate with the earth beneath it.

True luxury in travel is shifting away from this clinical isolation. Across the globe, a quieter movement is taking root: wellness that yields to terrain. When treatment rooms dissolve into volcanic horizons, subterranean limestone, dark sky reserves, and open ocean, the landscape ceases to be a mere backdrop. It becomes the primary practitioner, driving a nervous system reset that no white-noise machine can mimic.

Here are four destinations where physical geography is the ritual.

1. The Volcanic Mirror: Lake Atitlán, Guatemala

The Property: Casa Palopó

The Terrain: Volcanic caldera, altitude, and sacred waters

Perched on a steep, sun-washed cliff above Lake Atitlán, Casa Palopó—a 15-room Relais & Châteaux sanctuary—offers an immediate antidote to sensory overload. There are no televisions on the property. Instead, the architectural focus points entirely outward, framing the dramatic tripartite silhouette of Atitlán, Tolimán, and San Pedro volcanoes rising straight out of the water.

Atitlán is an ancient volcanic caldera, formed eighty thousand years ago in a collapse that created a natural amphitheater of raw earth energy. Here, stillness feels heavy and ancestral.

Rather than confining guests inside, wellness at Casa Palopó is tied to the elemental pull of the lake. Days begin with volcano-framed meditation on panoramic terraces, where the morning wind—the Xocomil—stirs the surface. At the newly opened Saq’ Ya’ Spa (“Blessed Water”), treatments incorporate local volcanic clay, indigenous botanicals, and river stones.

The centerpiece of the experience, however, is a traditional blessing ritual led by a local Mayan Shaman (Ajq’ij). Held out under the open sky, smoke from copal resin and local herbs drifts toward the peaks as ancestral chants anchor you firmly to the soil.

The Reset: The absence of artificial noise combined with the sheer scale of the caldera forces a rapid shift from hyper-vigilance to peripheral calm—a physical grounding that only a landscape born of deep earth forces can command.

2. The Celestial Chamber: South Iceland

The Property: Hotel Rangá

The Terrain: Glacial plains, geothermal water, and pristine dark skies

Located along the quiet banks of the Rangá River in southern Iceland, Hotel Rangá sits surrounded by vast, unpopulated volcanic plains. With the active volcano Hekla looming in the distance and near-zero light pollution, the property’s geography is defined by expanse, silence, and sky.

While conventional luxury spas rely on indoor hydrotherapy, Hotel Rangá turns the sub-Arctic environment into an open-air sanctuary. The ritual begins after dark in the outdoor geothermal hot tubs, fed directly by the island’s heated subterranean waters. As sub-zero air cools your forehead, mineral-dense water warms your body to its core—a stark, invigorating contrast that triggers immediate circulatory relief.

The experience expands during The Ultimate Star Bath. Soaking beneath the northern constellations—and often the shimmering ribbons of the Aurora Borealis—guests are joined by a resident astronomer for private celestial viewing.

The hotel complements this outdoor immersion with quiet analog touches indoors: custom astronomical mapping of the night sky above your room, a “Poetry Hotline,” and a fireside book turndown service that encourages reflection long after stepping out of the water.

The Reset: Staring into an unpolluted night sky while suspended in geothermal water shifts psychological perspective, reducing systemic stress through what neuroscientists term the “overview effect”—a sense of awe that recalibrates the mind.

3. The Subterranean Vault: Napa Valley, California

The Property: The Meritage Resort & Spa

The Terrain: Subterranean tufa limestone and terraced vineyards

While Napa Valley is typically associated with sun-drenched vineyard tours, its deepest restoration lies underground. Tucked beneath nine acres of active hillside vines, Spa Terra sits entirely within a 22,000-square-foot estate cave carved straight into the rock.

Stepping into the cave requires an instant sensory adjustment. The natural insulation of the earth keeps the air cool, quiet, and thick with the faint scent of stone and cedar. The absence of natural light eliminates circadian visual cues, allowing the nervous system to drop its guard.

Deep inside the stone walls, therapeutic massages and seasonal organic facials leverage local grape-seed oils rich in polyphenols.

Above ground, the resort uses the surrounding agricultural terroir for an ‘outside-in’ approach. Moonlight in the Vines gathers guests among the active vineyard rows under a full moon for guided breathwork and sound baths using crystal singing bowls. The sound waves travel through the cool night air and echo off the hillsides, grounding movement and breath directly into the agricultural cycle of the valley. Note: While Moonlight in the Vineyards is currently taking place outdoors, they will be moving the experience underground as the weather cools, trading the vineyards for the cozy, quiet setting of the Estate Cave during the full moon.

The Reset: The subterranean environment acts as a natural sensory deprivation chamber. Encased in stone, the brain stops scanning for environmental shifts, enabling a level of restorative sleep and muscle release that daylight spaces rarely afford.

4. The Pelagic Horizon: The Caribbean & Mediterranean

The Property: SeaDream Yacht Club

The Terrain: Open ocean, maritime breeze, and isolated sea coves

There is a distinct psychological difference between a massive ocean liner and a 112-guest mega-yacht like SeaDream I or II. Because of its nimble scale, SeaDream navigates away from commercial cruise tracks, anchoring in shallow, secluded harbors—from the quiet coves of the Dalmatian Coast to hidden bays in the Grenadines.

Onboard, the ocean itself acts as the wellness practitioner. SeaDream pioneered healthy dining at sea with a dedicated raw and plant-based menu alongside destination-inspired cuisine utilizing ingredients sourced at morning port stops. The yacht also features the only Thai-certified spa at sea, where treatments are conducted to the actual rhythm of ocean swells.

The ultimate landscape ritual happens at night through SeaDream’s signature Balinese Dream Beds. Positioned high on the open top deck, these plush, velvet-covered beds allow guests to spend the night sleeping under a canopy of stars as the vessel sails quietly between islands.

Unprotected by glass or steel, wrapped in sea air and lulled by the constant, low-frequency movement of the water, sleep becomes an immersive maritime experience.

The Reset: The gentle rolling motion of the sea synchronizes with slow-wave brain activity, while the unobstructed horizon line gives the optic nerve a rare chance to relax completely without structural barriers.

item.title: In Search of the Ideal
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Red-tailed hawks soar in wide loops over the Hudson Valley’s tapestry of emerald hemlock forests, golden fields, and rolling orchards. From high on the ridge at Olana, the river below catches the sun like an idealized ribbon of polished silver—until you walk down to the bank, where the illusion yields to raw texture, and the water proves dark, deep, and brackish. On the hilltop, the breeze off the butterfly garden carries sweet wisps of bergamot and lavender, brushing against the striking facade of Olana itself: an eclectic, Persian-inspired mansion of polychrome brick that is cut from an entirely different cloth than the Dutch farmsteads below. This was the home of Frederic Edwin Church, born 200 years ago in 1826, who spent his life capturing—and orchestrating—that very tension between raw wilderness and curated vision.

As America celebrates his bicentennial anniversary, I set out to re-examine his legacy and the broader Hudson River School across the region I’ve lived in for most of my life.

I’ll admit, my taste usually skews toward modern and contemporary art—I’m generally drawn to clean abstraction and conceptual work over 19th-century oil paintings. But tracing this movement across its original geography forced a shift in perspective. Seeing these works in context, you realize they weren’t just decorative landscapes; they were deliberate, highly engineered responses to a changing world.

The Route: Tracing the Canvas Across Upstate

Stop 1: The Foundation — Albany Institute of History & Art

To understand what the Hudson River School was truly reacting against, start in the heart of the capital at the Albany Institute of History & Art. Beyond its sweeping survey of early American art, the museum’s collection reveals the subtle ideological tensions of 19th-century New York. Stand before their Hudson River School canvases—particularly the depictions of Lake George, Otsego Lake, and a striking 1830s distant view of Troy. In that canvas, Troy sits low on the horizon, dark, shadowy, and nondescript beneath a mantle of industrial haze, while the foreground bursts with vivid, luminous flora and pristine nature—a visual manifesto prioritizing the wild ideal over industrial progress.

Stop 2: The Northern Sanctuary — Lake George

Heading north brings you to the waters of Lake George. Thomas Jefferson famously declared it “without comparison, the most beautiful water I ever saw”—a 32-mile stretch of crystal-clear alpine water framed by steep, forested Adirondack peaks. For Hudson River School artists like John Frederick Kensett and Asher Brown Durand, Lake George was the ultimate outdoor studio. They depicted it with a serene, atmospheric stillness (”luminism”), capturing the mirror-like reflections and misty morning light that made the lake feel like an untouched sanctuary.

Stop 3: The Storybook Setting — Cooperstown & The Fenimore

West in Cooperstown, nature and narrative intertw on the shores of Otsego Lake. Standing at the water’s edge and looking across the expanse, if you squint, you can just make out the distant stone tower on the far bank—barely a speck to the naked eye. Yet inside the Fenimore Art Museum, that same landscape takes on mythic proportions. The collection features masterworks by Thomas Cole, Asher Brown Durand, and their contemporaries, illustrating how these painters didn’t merely document a location, but romanticized it to echo James Fenimore Cooper’s literary world.

Stop 4: The Vantage Point — Hudson & The Rip Van Winkle Bridge

Heading south into Columbia County, the real heart of the movement comes into focus around the town of Hudson. Before crossing the river, head to the Rip Van Winkle Bridge Historic Walkway or the Catskill Mountain House Site overlook at North-South Lake. Standing high above the valley floor, you take in the exact panoramic vista of the Hudson winding through the hemlock canopy that inspired Cole’s first sketches in 1825—the true physical birthplace of the movement.

Stop 5: The Sacred Wilderness — Kaaterskill Falls

Before crossing back over the river, take the short drive up Route 23A into the clove to hike Kaaterskill Falls. This two-tiered, 260-foot waterfall is ground zero for the Hudson River School. Standing at the viewing platform or descending the stone steps into the natural amphitheater of the upper fall, you are looking at the exact scene Thomas Cole painted in 1825—a canvas that captivated the New York art world and launched the movement. While 19th-century tourists needed a local guide and a steep climb, today’s well-maintained trails allow you to easily experience the cool mist, towering hemlocks, and dramatic rock ledges that came to define the romantic American wilderness.

Stop 6: The Mentor’s Refuge — Thomas Cole National Historic Site (Cedar Grove)

Across the river in Catskill sits Cedar Grove, the home and studio of Thomas Cole. The yellow Federal-style house and his restored “New Studio” offer an intimate glimpse into the mind of the school’s founding father. It was here that a young Frederic Church arrived as a student in 1844, learning not just how to paint trees and skies, but how to compose grand moral and environmental allegories out of American soil.

Stop 7: The Masterpiece — Olana State Historic Site

Save a full day for Olana. Church’s home is less a house and more a 250-acre living sculpture. Spend the morning touring the Persian-inspired villa with its hand-painted tiles and orientalist interiors, then spend the afternoon walking the miles of engineered carriage roads. Pack a picnic to enjoy on the lawn overlooking the Hudson, where Church meticulously cleared trees and constructed an artificial lake to frame the ultimate, living composite landscape.

Where to Stay & Eat in Hudson

Savor & Sip:

Governor’s Tavern: A warm, unpretentious local staple offering outstanding burgers, high-end pub classics, and a great draft selection in a classic neighborhood tavern atmosphere.

Wm. Farmer and Sons: A quintessential Hudson institution offering exceptional craft cocktails, local draft beers, and high-end pub fare in a cozy, rustic-chic tavern setting.

Swoon Kitchenbar: A vibrant brasserie on Warren Street celebrated for its seasonal, farm-to-table menu and great wine list.

Where to Stay:

The Maker Hotel: A 2025 Michelin Key recipient, this exquisitely designed boutique hotel on Warren Street is a masterclass in bohemian luxury, celebrating local artisans, craftsmen, and timeless Hudson Valley style.
